intro: Willistown Township, in Chester County west of Philadelphia, is rolling farm and woodland cut by Crum Creek, with quiet suburban streets on its edge by Malvern. One reader has sent us four big trees here: an American sycamore about 6.5 metres round by the stone bridge where White Horse Road crosses the creek, white oaks on Bryan Avenue and Grubb Road, and a tall oak beside the 1793 Quaker meetinghouse. Look at the first three from the road; the meetinghouse oak stands on its lawn.
meta_description: Four big trees a reader sent from Willistown, Pennsylvania: a sycamore by the Crum Creek bridge, two white oaks and the oak at the Quaker meetinghouse.

trees.name: The Sycamore at the Crum Creek Bridge

location.address: Beside White Horse Road at its bridge over Crum Creek, Willistown Township, Chester County, PA

trees.story:
A reader put a tape round this sycamore and got about 6.5 metres. That is a big trunk for any tree in Pennsylvania, and the American sycamore is counted among the largest broadleaf trees of the eastern United States. They like exactly this kind of place, a creek bank with water close to the roots.

The reader who sent it called it "so massive and robust" and placed it "near an old stone bridge over Crum Creek, Willistown Township, closer to Paoli, not very near Media". Their pin lands on the spot where White Horse Road crosses the creek. Nobody we have read has written about this tree, so we do not know its age, who planted it, or whether it was planted at all. A sycamore this broad by a creek is often a seedling that simply found good ground.

Their photographs, taken in autumn sun, show the pale upper limbs that give the species away, the mottled grey bark lower down, and a base that flares out over a grassy bank beside a split-rail fence. If you go, look from the road side and leave the fences alone; we do not know who owns the ground it grows on. If you know its history, or have measured it yourself, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: A broad sycamore with pale, almost white upper limbs and mottled grey bark, its base flaring over a grassy bank beside a split-rail fence, by the stone bridge where White Horse Road crosses Crum Creek.
verified_sources: A reader's photographs and note through the app, 2026-11-15, with a pin they placed by hand at the White Horse Road bridge over Crum Creek
trees.verify_notes: 2026-11-15: sent by a reader through the app with two photographs (whole tree in autumn colour, trunk base), girth 650 cm by their measure, note: near an old stone bridge over Crum Creek, Willistown Township, closer to Paoli, not very near Media. Pin placed by hand, no GPS fix; it reverse-geocodes (Nominatim) exactly onto the White Horse Road bridge over Crum Creek (OSM way 74635054, bridge=yes), which matches the note; a stone wall at the right edge of the first photograph fits a bridge parapet. No written source found (searches for the bridge, the township, the Willistown Conservation Trust; not in the Pennsylvania champion lists we hold). Species from the photographs: pale upper limbs, plane-type bark and leaves; the reader also named it American sycamore. Ownership of the ground not known; access line tells visitors to look from the road. Published on Hidde's rule that a stranger's good photograph of a tree worth the walk is not held for a written source; precision approximate because the pin was placed by hand. Not the Tyler Arboretum trees in media-pennsylvania (about 9.6 km south-east).

trees.name: The White Oak of Bryan Avenue
trees.age_estimate: more than 300 years, by a reader's estimate

location.address: Bryan Avenue, Duffryn Mawr, Willistown Township, Chester County, PA 19355

trees.story:
"The spread of this oak is half the front lawn of this house," wrote the reader who sent it to us from Bryan Avenue, a quiet residential street in the Duffryn Mawr corner of Willistown Township, Chester County.

Their photographs bear that out. The trunk is short and massive, its pale grey bark broken into long shallow plates and swollen with burrs, and only a few metres up it splits into a crown of thick, crooked limbs. They run out almost level over the grass, one of them reaching past the roof of the low house behind, and with most of the leaves down in November you can follow every bend of them against the sky. The last leaves hang on in rusty red, the way a white oak holds its foliage late into autumn.

The reader puts it at more than 300 years old and its girth at about 510 centimetres. Those figures are theirs; we have found nothing written about this tree. If they are right, the oak was growing here long before the street was laid out around it. If you know its history, or the story the neighbours tell about it, tell us.

It stands on a private front lawn. Look at it from the street, and leave the garden to the people who live there.
trees.how_to_recognise: A huge, low-branched oak alone on a front lawn on Bryan Avenue: a short pale trunk with burrs on it, splitting a few metres up into thick crooked limbs that reach out over the grass and past the roof of the low grey house behind.
verified_sources: A reader's three photographs and note through the app, 2026-11-20, with a pin they placed by hand on Bryan Avenue, Willistown Township
trees.access: Seen from Bryan Avenue. The lawn it stands on is a private front garden, so stay on the street.

trees.name: The White Oak on Grubb Road
trees.age_estimate: about 225 years, by a reader's estimate

location.address: Beside Grubb Road, Duffryn Mawr, Willistown Township, Chester County, PA 19355

trees.story:
"This splendid white oak hugs the inclined bank on the side of the road on the edge of split rail fenced meadow," wrote the reader who sent it to us from Grubb Road in Willistown Township, Chester County. It is the third big tree they have found for us here, half a kilometre from their sycamore at the Crum Creek bridge.

Their photograph, taken on a bright August day with their bicycle on its kickstand by the fence, looks up from the foot of the bank. The trunk is grey and deeply furrowed, flaring at the base where its roots grip the slope, and a few metres up it splits into great crooked limbs. One of them runs out almost level over the meadow behind the rails before turning up into a high, open crown full of light.

The reader puts its girth at 435 centimetres and its age at about 225 years. Those figures are theirs; we have found nothing written about this oak, and nobody we have read has measured it. If you know its story, or what the neighbours call it, tell us and we will add it.

Look at it from the roadside, where the reader stood, and leave the meadow fence alone. Summer is the time to see the crown at its fullest, as in their picture.
trees.how_to_recognise: On a sloping bank beside Grubb Road: a grey, furrowed oak trunk with an old rust-red sign on it, its roots gripping the slope, a split-rail fence behind it, and one long limb reaching out level over the field.

trees.access: Seen from Grubb Road, on the bank at the roadside. The meadow behind the fence is not known to be public, so stay on the road side and take care with traffic.

trees.name: The Meetinghouse Oak of Willistown
trees.age_estimate: more than 150 years, by a reader's estimate

location.address: Grounds of the Willistown Friends Meetinghouse, Willistown Township, Chester County, PA

trees.story:
"The biggest mightiest tree, another oak, was taken down to allow for a building expansion," wrote the reader who sent us this one from the grounds of the Willistown Friends Meetinghouse in Chester County. What still stands is this oak, south-west of the meetinghouse, which the reader dates to 1793: look for the year below the peak of the east gable.

Their photograph, taken on a November afternoon, shows how tall it has grown in the open. A single grey trunk rises from a lawn deep in fallen leaves and runs straight for a long way before it branches into a tall, narrow crown. The lower half still holds its leaves, brown and papery, while the top is already bare against the clouds. Keeping dead leaves on the lower branches into winter is a habit of the pin oaks, and the reader knows it as a northern pin oak; tell us if you can confirm which.

The reader puts its girth at 400 centimetres and its age at more than 150 years. Those figures are theirs; we have found nothing written about this tree.

They also send visitors on to the open buggy shed west of the meetinghouse, where planks are stacked for drying. Walk round the trunk first, then step back towards the meetinghouse to see the whole crown.
trees.how_to_recognise: On the lawn south-west of the meetinghouse: a tall, straight grey oak whose lower branches keep their brown leaves into winter, a split-rail fence and small stone pillar to its left, a smaller oak and bench to its right.

trees.verify_notes: 2026-11-23 reader judge: sent by a reader through the app (ca6ba683-9ff8-4de1-adf3-d8f2055e898d). Photograph viewed: the whole tall oak on a lawn deep in fallen leaves, a straight grey trunk, the lower crown still in brown leaves and the top bare, a split-rail fence and small stone pillar to the left, a smaller oak with a bench to the right, November daylight, colour. The reader's own figures: name 'Northern Pin Oak at Willistown Friends - Quaker Meetinghouse', species 'Northern Pin Oak', age '150+', girth 400 cm; their note names the 1793 date on the meetinghouse's east gable, a bigger oak taken down for a building expansion, and planks drying in the buggy shed. A second photograph they sent shows those stacked planks, not the tree, so it is not on the page. Species left as Quercus sp.: the reader says northern pin oak (Q. ellipsoidalis), which is a Midwestern species; the retained lower leaves and the habit look like pin oak (Q. palustris). Published under the closed list for a reader's tree (Hidde, 2026-11-17); approximate because the pin was placed by hand. Same reader as wtn_001 to wtn_003. No register entry within 100 m.

question_meta: The biggest trees readers found in Willistown, PA: a sycamore by Crum Creek, two white oaks, the Quaker meetinghouse oak, and where to look.
question_answer: Readers have sent us four big trees in Willistown Township, Chester County. An American sycamore stands by the old stone bridge where White Horse Road crosses Crum Creek, about 650 cm round by a reader's measure. A white oak on Bryan Avenue in Duffryn Mawr is about 510 cm round and more than 300 years old by a reader's estimate, and another beside Grubb Road is about 435 cm round and about 225 years old by the same reader's figures. A tall oak on the grounds of the Willistown Friends Meetinghouse is about 400 cm round. No age has been published for any of them.
question_context: All four trees came to us from one reader through the app in November 2026, with photographs and their own measurements. The sycamore grows near an old stone bridge over Crum Creek, its base on a grassy bank beside a split-rail fence; the species is counted among the largest broadleaf trees of the eastern United States and favours creek banks like this one. Half a kilometre north-west, a white oak hugs the sloping bank of Grubb Road at the edge of a fenced meadow. The other white oak is about two kilometres further north-west, on a front lawn on Bryan Avenue near Malvern, and the reader puts it at more than 300 years old. The fourth stands about three kilometres south of the bridge, on the lawn south-west of the Willistown Friends Meetinghouse, which the reader dates to 1793; a bigger oak beside it was taken down for a building expansion. We have found nothing written about any of them, so the reader's figures are the only ones.

faq.a: The sycamore is about 650 cm round, the Bryan Avenue white oak about 510 cm, the Grubb Road white oak about 435 cm and the meetinghouse oak about 400 cm, all by the measure of the reader who sent them. Nobody else has published a figure.

The reader puts the Bryan Avenue oak at more than 300 years, the Grubb Road oak at about 225 and the meetinghouse oak at more than 150. Nobody has published an age for any of them. If you know their history, tell us.

The sycamore is beside White Horse Road at its stone bridge over Crum Creek, the Grubb Road oak on the roadside bank half a kilometre north-west of it, the Bryan Avenue oak on a front lawn in Duffryn Mawr, and the meetinghouse oak on the lawn of the Willistown Friends Meetinghouse. All four pins are approximate. See the first three from the road.
